lines.text:
Ceremony, Tradition, and the Language of Commitment

A wedding is a contract dressed in ritual. Beneath the flowers, the music, and the emotion lies a legal and social act: two people making vows before witnesses and an officiant. Yet the ceremony's power comes not from the contract but from the theatre that surrounds it — the slow walk down the aisle, the exchange of rings at the altar, the blessing, the kiss, and the recessional as the couple walks back through their gathered community.

The cast of characters is precise. The bride and groom stand at the centre. A best man holds the rings. A maid of honour adjusts the veil. Bridesmaids and groomsmen flank the couple. A flower girl scatters petals along the aisle. A ring bearer carries the bands on a cushion. The photographer moves silently, capturing moments that will outlast the day. An officiant — religious or civil — presides, guiding the couple through their vows, a reading, and the lighting of a unity candle.

Wedding attire carries symbolic weight. The wedding dress — traditionally white in Western cultures — has evolved from a marker of social status into a personal statement. A veil frames the face. A tiara catches the light. The groom's tuxedo or suit is matched by a boutonniere pinned to the lapel. Cufflinks, a bow tie, and polished shoes complete the look. The bride's bouquet — often chosen to match the floral arch — is tossed to unmarried guests at the reception.

The reception transforms ceremony into celebration. A seating chart directs guests to their tables. A table setting — plates, glasses, cutlery, napkins — is arranged around a centrepiece of flowers and candles. A table runner marks each long table. The caterer serves the meal. A toast — delivered by the best man, then the parents — raises glasses in honour of the couple. The first dance clears the dance floor. A band or DJ keeps it full until midnight. A photo booth, fairy lights, lanterns, and sparklers create atmosphere. Confetti rains at the exit.

Behind the scenes, months of planning converge on a single day. An invitation includes the venue, date, and an RSVP card. A florist designs the arrangements. A menu balances dietary needs. A guest book collects handwritten messages. A gift table overflows. A DJ booth anchors one corner of the room; a ribbon marks the boundary of the dance floor.

Wedding traditions vary enormously across cultures. In many Muslim ceremonies, a mahr (bridal gift) is agreed upon, and the nikah contract is signed before witnesses. In Hindu weddings, the couple circles a sacred fire. In Japanese Shinto ceremonies, sake is shared from three cups. In Nigerian Yoruba weddings, the groom prostrates before the bride's family. What remains constant is the public nature of the commitment — the act of standing before family and community and declaring intention aloud.

The language of weddings — vows, blessings, toasts — belongs to a formal register rarely encountered in daily life. Mastering it means understanding not just vocabulary but the social weight each word carries.

lines.text: 'Marry' is transitive — it needs an object: 'He married her.' Without an object, use 'get married' or 'be married': 'They got married last summer.' 'They were married by a judge.' 'Marry' without object (*they married) is non-standard in British English and formal American English.

lines.text: 'On' + specific date: 'on the 15th of June', 'on Saturday'. 'In' + month alone: 'in June'. 'At' + venue/time: 'at the Grand Hotel', 'at 3pm'. When date and month appear together, 'on' governs: 'on the 15th of June' (not *in the 15th June).

lines.text: 'Neither...nor' and 'either...or' are fixed correlative pairs. Never mix them: *neither...or, *either...nor. 'Neither the venue nor the food disappointed.' lines.text: 'Everyone', 'everybody', 'everything', 'no one', 'nobody' take singular verbs: 'Everyone was crying', 'Nobody has arrived', 'Everything is ready.' Despite referring to multiple people, these pronouns are grammatically singular. The same applies to 'each', 'every', and 'neither' as subjects.

lines.text: An Islamic wedding (nikah) centres on the marriage contract signed by the couple in the presence of witnesses and an imam. The mahr (dowry) is given by the groom to the bride. The walima is the wedding feast, often held the day after the nikah. Men and women may celebrate separately, and there is typically no alcohol. Modesty in dress is observed throughout.
lines.name: An Islamic wedding (nikah) centres on the marriage contract signed by the couple in the presence of witnesses and an imam. The mahr (dowry) is given by the groom to the bride. The walima is the wedding feast, often held the day after the nikah. Men and women may celebrate separately, and there is typically no alcohol. Modesty in dress is observed throughout.

lines.text: In British English, the formal meal at a wedding reception is called the 'wedding breakfast' — even though it's usually served in the afternoon or evening. The name comes from the fact that it's the first meal the couple eat together as married people — they 'break their fast' from the ceremony. This confuses many English learners.

lines.text: Best Man and Maid of Honour
lines.name: Best Man and Maid of Honour

lines.text: The 'best man' (groom's closest friend/relative) and 'maid of honour' (bride's closest friend/relative — 'matron of honour' if married) are key roles. The best man traditionally gives a humorous speech, often gently embarrassing the groom with stories. The maid of honour helps the bride prepare and organises the hen party.
lines.name: The 'best man' (groom's closest friend/relative) and 'maid of honour' (bride's closest friend/relative — 'matron of honour' if married) are key roles. The best man traditionally gives a humorous speech, often gently embarrassing the groom with stories. The maid of honour helps the bride prepare and organises the hen party.

lines.text: A 'hen party' (or 'hen do') is a pre-wedding celebration for the bride with her friends. A 'stag party' (or 'stag do') is the groom's equivalent. In American English: 'bachelorette party' and 'bachelor party'. These often involve a weekend away, activities, and matching outfits. They're typically held one to four weeks before the wedding.
